decision.explanation: Reversing the limits gives ∫₃⁵ f(x) dx = 5. Thus ∫₃⁵ (5 − 4f(x)) dx = 5(5 − 3) − 4(5) = −10.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{5}^{3}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factoring out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{5}(5-4f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{3}^{5}\text{d}x-4{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x{|}_{3}^{5}-4(5) \\  & =5(5-3)-20 \\  & =10-20 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2$ and ${\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=3,$ then what is ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x?$
after.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2+3 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 1 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =1+2\cdot x\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =1+2(3-0) \\  & =1+6 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$
